claim: CLN4 is an autosomal dominant neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis caused by mutations in the synaptic vesicle protein CSPα.
source: The autosomal dominant neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCL) CLN4 is caused by mutations in the synaptic vesicle (SV) protein CSPα.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the introduction.

claim: CLN4 mutations induced excessive oligomerization of hCSPα in Drosophila neurons.
source: Similar to patients, CLN4 mutations induced excessive oligomerization of hCSPα and premature lethality in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing high-molecular weight oligomers in Figure 2A.

claim: CLN4 mutations caused premature lethality in Drosophila in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Similar to patients, CLN4 mutations induced excessive oligomerization of hCSPα and premature lethality in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 3A showing reduced viability with two-copy expression.

claim: Most CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulated abnormally instead of being localized to synaptic vesicles.
source: Instead of being localized to SVs, most CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulated abnormally, and co-localized with ubiquitinated proteins and the prelysosomal markers HRS and LAMP1.
evidence: Shown by immunostaining data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: CLN4 mutant hCSPα co-localized with ubiquitinated proteins.
source: Instead of being localized to SVs, most CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulated abnormally, and co-localized with ubiquitinated proteins and the prelysosomal markers HRS and LAMP1.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 4D, F.

claim: CLN4 mutant hCSPα co-localized with the prelysosomal markers HRS and LAMP1.
source: Instead of being localized to SVs, most CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulated abnormally, and co-localized with ubiquitinated proteins and the prelysosomal markers HRS and LAMP1.
evidence: Shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 5B, E, F.

claim: Ultrastructural examination revealed frequent abnormal membrane structures in axons and neuronal somata of CLN4 mutants.
source: Ultrastructural examination revealed frequent abnormal membrane structures in axons and neuronal somata.
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 6.

claim: Reducing endogenous wild type dCSP levels attenuated the lethality induced by CLN4 mutations.
source: The lethality, oligomerization and prelysosomal accumulation induced by CLN4 mutations was attenuated by reducing endogenous wild type (WT) dCSP levels and enhanced by increasing WT levels.
evidence: Shown by viability data in Figure 7A.

claim: Increasing wild type CSP levels enhanced the lethality induced by CLN4 mutations.
source: The lethality, oligomerization and prelysosomal accumulation induced by CLN4 mutations was attenuated by reducing endogenous wild type (WT) dCSP levels and enhanced by increasing WT levels.
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Reducing endogenous wild type dCSP levels attenuated oligomerization of CLN4 mutant hCSPα.
source: The lethality, oligomerization and prelysosomal accumulation induced by CLN4 mutations was attenuated by reducing endogenous wild type (WT) dCSP levels and enhanced by increasing WT levels.
evidence: Shown by Western blot data in Figure 7D, F.

claim: Increasing wild type CSP levels enhanced oligomerization of CLN4 mutant hCSPα.
source: The lethality, oligomerization and prelysosomal accumulation induced by CLN4 mutations was attenuated by reducing endogenous wild type (WT) dCSP levels and enhanced by increasing WT levels.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 7E, I, L.

claim: Reducing the gene dosage of Hsc70 attenuated CLN4 phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, reducing the gene dosage of Hsc70 also attenuated CLN4 phenotypes.
evidence: Shown by multiple assays in Figure 9 including eye phenotypes, viability, and oligomerization.

claim: CLN4 alleles resemble dominant hypermorphic gain of function mutations that drive excessive oligomerization and impair membrane trafficking.
source: Taken together, we suggest that CLN4 alleles resemble dominant hypermorphic gain of function mutations that drive excessive oligomerization and impair membrane trafficking.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic interaction data showing that reducing WT CSP suppresses rather than enhances phenotypes, which is inconsistent with dominant-negative effects.

claim: NCLs comprise a group of progressive neurodegenerative diseases with 14 known disease-associated genes, termed CLN1-14.
source: NCLs comprise a group of progressive neurodegenerative diseases with 14 known disease-associated genes, termed CLN1-14 (Haltia, 2003; Haltia and Goebel, 2013; Jalanko and Braulke, 2009; Mole and Cotman, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: NCLs have mostly an infantile or juvenile symptomatic onset and are characterized by loss of vision, gait abnormalities, seizures, dementia, and premature death.
source: NCLs have mostly an infantile or juvenile symptomatic onset and are characterized by loss of vision, gait abnormalities, seizures, dementia, and premature death.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about NCLs.

claim: NCLs are generally considered lysosomal storage diseases due to the accumulation of lipofuscin.
source: In general, NCLs are considered lysosomal storage diseases due the accumulation of lipofuscin and are typically caused by recessive loss of function mutations with one exception, CLN4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NCL classification.

claim: Most NCLs are caused by recessive loss of function mutations with one exception, CLN4.
source: In general, NCLs are considered lysosomal storage diseases due the accumulation of lipofuscin and are typically caused by recessive loss of function mutations with one exception, CLN4.
evidence: This distinguishes CLN4 from other NCLs based on inheritance pattern.

claim: The autosomal dominantly inherited NCL CLN4 has an adult onset between 25 and 46 years.
source: The autosomal dominantly inherited NCL CLN4 has an adult onset between 25 and 46 years.
evidence: This is clinical information about CLN4 disease onset.

claim: CLN4 is caused by either the amino acid substitution L115R or the single amino acid deletion L116Δ in the SV protein CSPα.
source: CLN4 is caused by either the amino acid (aa) substitution L115R or the single amino acid deletion L116Δ in the SV protein CSPα, which is encoded by the human DNAJC5 gene (Benitez et al., 2011; Cadieux-Dion et al., 2013; Nosková et al., 2011; Velinov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of CLN4 supported by multiple citations.

claim: CSPα is encoded by the human DNAJC5 gene.
source: CLN4 is caused by either the amino acid (aa) substitution L115R or the single amino acid deletion L116Δ in the SV protein CSPα, which is encoded by the human DNAJC5 gene (Benitez et al., 2011; Cadieux-Dion et al., 2013; Nosková et al., 2011; Velinov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established genetic nomenclature.

claim: CSPα is unique among NCL-associated genes since it encodes a SV protein with no known lysosome-associated functions.
source: CSPα is unique among NCL-associated genes since it encodes a SV protein with no known lysosome-associated functions.
evidence: This distinguishes CSPα from other NCL-associated proteins.

claim: There is no CLN4 model explaining lysosomal failure.
source: Accordingly, there is no CLN4 model explaining lysosomal failure.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: CSPα is an evolutionary conserved neuroprotective co-chaperone of Hsc70.
source: CSPα is an evolutionary conserved neuroprotective co-chaperone of Hsc70 and required to maintain synaptic function and prevent neurodegeneration (Burgoyne and Morgan, 2011; Burgoyne and Morgan, 2015; Zinsmaier, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CSPα function supported by citations.

claim: CSPα is required to maintain synaptic function and prevent neurodegeneration.
source: CSPα is an evolutionary conserved neuroprotective co-chaperone of Hsc70 and required to maintain synaptic function and prevent neurodegeneration (Burgoyne and Morgan, 2011; Burgoyne and Morgan, 2015; Zinsmaier, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CSPα function supported by citations.

claim: Gene deletions of CSP in flies and mice cause progressive locomotor defects, paralysis and premature death due to neurodegeneration.
source: Gene deletions in flies and mice cause progressive locomotor defects, paralysis and premature death due to neurodegeneration (Chandra et al., 2005; Fernández-Chacón et al., 2004; Umbach et al., 1994; Zinsmaier, 2010; Zinsmaier et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: On SVs, CSPα forms a molecular chaperone complex with Hsc70 for a selected set of clients, which include SNARE proteins and dynamin.
source: On SVs, CSPα forms a molecular chaperone complex with Hsc70 for a selected set of clients, which include SNARE proteins and dynamin (Chandra et al., 2005; Nie et al., 1999; Sharma et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CSPα's molecular function supported by citations.

claim: Maintaining SNARE and dynamin function is likely key to CSP's neuroprotective role.
source: Maintaining SNARE and dynamin function is likely key to CSP's neuroprotective role (Burgoyne and Morgan, 2011; Rozas et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The CLN4 causing dominant mutations L115R and L116Δ are clustered in the palmitoylated cysteine-string (CS) domain of CSPα.
source: The CLN4 causing dominant mutations L115R and L116Δ are clustered in the palmitoylated cysteine-string (CS) domain of CSPα, which mediates CSPα's secretory trafficking to axon terminals, its SV association, and its dimerization (Arnold et al., 2004; Chamberlain and Burgoyne, 1998; Greaves and Chamberlain, 2006; Greaves et al., 2008; Ohyama et al., 2007; Stowers and Isacoff, 2007; Swayne et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the location of CLN4 mutations supported by citations.

claim: The CS domain mediates CSPα's secretory trafficking to axon terminals, its SV association, and its dimerization.
source: The CLN4 causing dominant mutations L115R and L116Δ are clustered in the palmitoylated cysteine-string (CS) domain of CSPα, which mediates CSPα's secretory trafficking to axon terminals, its SV association, and its dimerization (Arnold et al., 2004; Chamberlain and Burgoyne, 1998; Greaves and Chamberlain, 2006; Greaves et al., 2008; Ohyama et al., 2007; Stowers and Isacoff, 2007; Swayne et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CS domain function supported by citations.

claim: Palmitoylation of the CS domain enables CSPα's export from the ER and Golgi.
source: Palmitoylation of the CS domain enables CSPα's export from the ER and Golgi (Chamberlain and Burgoyne, 1998; Greaves and Chamberlain, 2006; Greaves et al., 2008; Ohyama et al., 2007; Stowers and Isacoff, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about palmitoylation's role supported by citations.

claim: Palmitoylation must be maintained for CSPα's association with synaptic vesicle precursors (SVPs) and/or SVs, presumably due to the short lifetime of palmitoylation.
source: Palmitoylation must then be maintained for CSPα's association with synaptic vesicle precursors (SVPs) and/or SVs, presumably to due to the short lifetime of palmitoylation (Fukata and Fukata, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited knowledge about palmitoylation dynamics.

claim: In a lysosomal disease mouse model of Mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA (MPS-IIIA), palmitoylation of CSPα was decreased and its proteasomal degradation was increased.
source: Notably, there is a link between CSPα's degree of lipidation and lysosomal dysfunction. In a lysosomal disease mouse model of Mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA (MPS-IIIA), palmitoylation of CSPα was decreased and its proteasomal degradation was increased (Sambri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Overexpression of CSPα in MPS-IIIA mice ameliorated their presynaptic defects, neurodegeneration, and prolonged survival.
source: Since overexpression (OE) of CSPα in MPS-IIIA mice ameliorated their presynaptic defects, neurodegeneration, and prolonged survival, CSPα could be a critical factor for the progression of many lysosomal diseases (Sambri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: CSPα could be a critical factor for the progression of many lysosomal diseases.
source: Since overexpression (OE) of CSPα in MPS-IIIA mice ameliorated their presynaptic defects, neurodegeneration, and prolonged survival, CSPα could be a critical factor for the progression of many lysosomal diseases (Sambri et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited experimental results.

claim: Post-mortem analysis of CLN4 patient brains suggests that dominant CLN4 mutations reduce monomeric levels of lipidated CSPα.
source: Post-mortem analysis of CLN4 patient brains suggests that dominant CLN4 mutations have two key pathological effects: to reduce monomeric levels of lipidated CSPα and promote the formation of high-molecular weight CSPα protein aggregates/oligomers that are ubiquitinated (Greaves et al., 2012; Henderson et al., 2016; Nosková et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited post-mortem studies.

claim: Dominant CLN4 mutations promote the formation of high-molecular weight CSPα protein aggregates/oligomers that are ubiquitinated.
source: Post-mortem analysis of CLN4 patient brains suggests that dominant CLN4 mutations have two key pathological effects: to reduce monomeric levels of lipidated CSPα and promote the formation of high-molecular weight CSPα protein aggregates/oligomers that are ubiquitinated (Greaves et al., 2012; Henderson et al., 2016; Nosková et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited post-mortem studies.

claim: Similar effects of CLN4 mutations were seen in HEK293T, PC12 cells, and fibroblasts from CLN4 carriers.
source: Similar effects of the mutations were seen in HEK293T, PC12 cells, and fibroblasts from CLN4 carriers (Benitez and Sands, 2017; Greaves et al., 2012; Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited cell culture studies.

claim: In vitro, CLN4 mutant CSPα aggregates form in a time-, concentration- and temperature-dependent manner.
source: In vitro, CLN4 mutant CSPα aggregates form in a time-, concentration- and temperature-dependent manner (Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited in vitro study.

claim: Palmitoylation of CSPα promotes aggregation.
source: Palmitoylation of CSPα promotes aggregation (Greaves et al., 2012), although it is not essential (Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Palmitoylation is not essential for CLN4 mutant CSPα aggregation.
source: Palmitoylation of CSPα promotes aggregation (Greaves et al., 2012), although it is not essential (Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Post-mortem brains of CLN4 patients exhibit large scale changes in protein palmitoylation.
source: In addition, post-mortem brains of CLN4 patients exhibit large scale changes in protein palmitoylation (Henderson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: CLN4 mutations have no adverse short-term effects on CSPα's co-chaperone functions in vitro, including activation of Hsc70's ATPase activity, or the binding to chaperone clients like SNAP25 and dynamin.
source: CLN4 mutations have no adverse short-term effects on CSPα's co-chaperone functions in vitro, including activation of Hsc70's ATPase activity, or the binding to chaperone clients like SNAP25 and dynamin (Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited in vitro study.

claim: During prolonged incubation, the ability of mutant CSPα to stimulate Hsc70's ATPase activity declines considerably.
source: However, during prolonged incubation, the ability of mutant CSPα to stimulate Hsc70's ATPase activity declines considerably (Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited in vitro study.

claim: One-year old heterozygous CSPα KO mice develop a moderate motor defect characterized by a reduced ability to sustain motor unit recruitment during repetitive stimulation.
source: Consistent with this possibility, one-year old heterozygous CSPα KO mice develop a moderate motor defect that is characterized by a reduced ability to sustain motor unit recruitment during repetitive stimulation (Lopez-Ortega et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Neuronally expressed hCSPα was efficiently trafficked to axon terminals and co-localized with endogenous dCSP in the neuropil of the larval ventral nerve cord.
source: Neuronally expressed hCSPα was efficiently trafficked to axon terminals and co-localized with endogenous dCSP in the neuropil of the larval ventral nerve cord (VNC; Figure 1B) and larval neuromuscular junctions (NMJs; Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining images in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Neuronally expressed hCSPα co-localized with endogenous dCSP at larval neuromuscular junctions.
source: Neuronally expressed hCSPα was efficiently trafficked to axon terminals and co-localized with endogenous dCSP in the neuropil of the larval ventral nerve cord (VNC; Figure 1B) and larval neuromuscular junctions (NMJs; Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining images in Figure 1C.

claim: The majority of neuronally expressed hCSPα was palmitoylated.
source: Consistent with the normal trafficking of hCSPα, the majority of neuronally expressed hCSPα was palmitoylated, which was confirmed by treating larval protein extracts with 0.5 M hydroxylamine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by hydroxylamine treatment assay in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pan-neuronal elav-driven expression of normal hCSPα from one transgenic copy in homozygous dcsp deletion mutants significantly restored adult lifespan from ~4–5 days to 15–20 days.
source: Pan-neuronal elav-driven expression of normal hCSPα from one transgenic copy in homozygous dcsp deletion mutants significantly restored adult lifespan from ~4–5 days to 15–20 days (LD50 p<0.001; Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by lifespan data in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of fly dCSP2 partially restored adult lifespan in dcsp deletion mutants.
source: In comparison, expression of fly dCSP2 also restored adult lifespan only partially (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by lifespan data in Figure 1D.

claim: hCSPα is functional in flies.
source: Even though this rescue was only partial, it confirms that hCSPα is functional in flies, which made a CLN4 Drosophila model using human proteins tenable.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of dcsp mutant phenotypes.

claim: Neuronal expression of hCSP-L115 and -L116 in a dcsp null background was able to partially rescue the lifespan deficit.
source: Notably, neuronal expression of hCSP-L115 and -L116 in a dcsp null background was able to partially rescue the lifespan deficit (p<0.001, LD50), although not nearly to the extent of WT hCSPα (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by lifespan data in Figure 1D.

claim: CLN4 mutant hCSPα proteins are at least partially functional.
source: This indicates that CLN4 mutant hCSPα proteins are at least partially functional.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of dcsp mutant phenotypes by CLN4 mutant hCSPα.

claim: Levels of lipidated monomeric hCSP-L115 and -L116 were significantly reduced to 13% and 40% of WT hCSPα levels, respectively.
source: In comparison, levels of lipidated monomeric hCSP-L115 and -L116 were significantly reduced to 13% and 40% of WT hCSPα levels, respectively (p<0.003, Figure 2A,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2A, D.

claim: Levels of lipidated hCSP-L115 monomers were significantly lower than hCSP-L116.
source: Levels of lipidated hCSP-L115 monomers were significantly lower than hCSP-L116 (p<0.01, Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2D.

claim: Levels of non-lipidated monomeric hCSP-L115 and -L116 were comparable to WT hCSPα levels.
source: Levels of non-lipidated monomeric hCSP-L115 and -L116 were comparable to WT hCSPα levels (p>0.2; Figure 2A,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2A, E.

claim: Both CLN4 mutations induced the formation of SDS-resistant, high-molecular weight hCSPα oligomers in Drosophila neurons.
source: Both CLN4 mutations induced the formation of SDS-resistant, high-molecular weight hCSPα oligomers in Drosophila neurons (p<0.002; Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 2A, C.

claim: WT hCSPα oligomers were barely detectable.
source: In contrast, WT hCSPα oligomers were barely detectable (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 2A, C.

claim: The mutation L115 triggered oligomerization to a significantly larger degree than L116.
source: The mutation L115 triggered oligomerization to a significantly larger degree than L116 (p<0.006; Figure 2C), which is consistent with the lower levels of hCSP-L115 monomers (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2C.

claim: Increasing levels of DTT in the buffer to reduce disulfide bonds had little to no effect on the levels and size of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers.
source: Increasing levels of DTT in the buffer to reduce disulfide bonds had little to no effect on the levels and size of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers, which varied widely from ~250 kDa to more than 500 kDa (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The anti-ubiquitinated protein antibody only recognized a strong ~250 kD protein band in precipitates from L115 and L116 mutant brains, which correlated in size with high-molecular weight hCSPα oligomers.
source: The anti-ubiquitinated protein antibody only recognized a strong ~250 kD protein band in precipitates from L115 and L116 mutant brains, which correlated in size with high-molecular weight hCSPα oligomers (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and Western blot in Figure 2B.

claim: No ubiquitin-positive signals corresponding to CLN4 mutant hCSPα monomers, WT hCSPα monomers or oligomers were detected.
source: No ubiquitin-positive signals corresponding to CLN4 mutant hCSPα monomers, WT hCSPα monomers or oligomers were detected (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and Western blot in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα in fly brains reproduces the critical biochemical pathological features of post-mortem human CLN4 brains.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα in fly brains reproduces the critical biochemical pathological features of post-mortem human CLN4 brains (Greaves et al., 2012; Henderson et al., 2016; Nosková et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing reduced monomers and increased ubiquitinated oligomers.

claim: Oligomerization of purified CLN4 mutant hCSPα proteins is dose-dependent in vitro.
source: Oligomerization of purified CLN4 mutant hCSPα proteins is dose-dependent in vitro (Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Doubling the gene dosage of WT hCSPα increased levels of lipidated and non-lipidated monomeric WT hCSPα ~2.4 fold and ~3.3 fold, respectively.
source: In comparison to the expression from one transgene, levels of lipidated and non-lipidated monomeric WT hCSPα increased ~2.4 fold and ~3.3 fold, respectively (p<0.01, Figure 2A,D–E,H–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2A, D-E, H-I.

claim: WT hCSP oligomer levels increased only 1.5-fold when gene dosage was doubled.
source: Yet, WT hCSP oligomer levels increased only 1.5-fold (p<0.005; Figure 2G) and remained low such that the oligomer/monomer ratio was not altered (p=0.9; Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2G, C.

claim: Doubling gene dosage increased levels of lipidated hCSP-L115 monomers only modestly by 1.5-fold.
source: In comparison to single copy gene expression, doubling gene dosage increased levels of lipidated hCSP-L115 monomers only modestly by 1.5-fold (p<0.04) while hCSP-L116 levels were not significantly affected (p=0.3; Figure 2H).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2H.

claim: Doubling gene dosage did not significantly affect lipidated hCSP-L116 monomer levels.
source: In comparison to single copy gene expression, doubling gene dosage increased levels of lipidated hCSP-L115 monomers only modestly by 1.5-fold (p<0.04) while hCSP-L116 levels were not significantly affected (p=0.3; Figure 2H).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2H.

claim: Levels of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers increased 4.6- and 3.6-fold, respectively, when gene dosage was doubled.
source: However, levels of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers increased 4.6- and 3.6-fold, respectively (p<0.04; Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2G.

claim: The oligomer/monomer ratio increased from 0.9 to 2.8 for hCSP-L115 and from 0.4 to 1.8 for hCSP-L116 when gene dosage was doubled.
source: Due to the disproportional increase of CLN4 mutant oligomers, the oligomer/monomer ratio increased from 0.9 to 2.8 for hCSP-L115 and from 0.4 to 1.8 for hCSP-L116 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2C.

claim: Oligomerization of hCSP-L115 and -L116 is dose-dependent.
source: Hence, oligomerization of hCSP-L115 and -L116 is dose-dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing increased oligomerization with increased gene dosage.

claim: Doubling expression disproportionally increased levels of non-lipidated hCSP-L115 and -L116 monomers 8.6- and 4.6-fold, respectively.
source: Doubling expression disproportionally increased levels of non-lipidated hCSP-L115 and -L116 monomers 8.6- and 4.6-fold, respectively (p<0.002, Figure 2I).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2I.

claim: Doubling gene dosage of hCSP-L115 and -L116 expression increased total overall protein levels 3.0 and 3.9-fold, respectively.
source: Doubling gene dosage of hCSP-L115 and -L116 expression increased total overall protein levels 3.0 and 3.9-fold, respectively (p<0.002; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Levels of endogenous dCSP monomers were not affected by low or high expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα.
source: Levels of endogenous dCSP monomers were not affected by low or high expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα (Figure 2J).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 2J.

claim: High-molecular weight oligomers of endogenous WT dCSP were not detectable after expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα.
source: Notably, high-molecular weight oligomers of endogenous WT dCSP were not detectable after expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), which contrasts a previous study detecting small amounts of overexpressed GFP-tagged WT hCSPα in CLN4 mutant hCSPα oligomers (Greaves et al., 2012).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Elav-driven neuronal expression of WT or CLN4 mutant hCSPα from a single transgene had no effect on viability during development.
source: Elav-driven neuronal expression of WT or CLN4 mutant hCSPα from a single transgene had no effect on viability during development (Figure 3A) and adult lifespan (not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 3A.

claim: Doubling gene expression levels severely reduced viability during development of hCSP-L115 and -L116 animals in comparison to WT hCSPα expression.
source: However, doubling gene expression levels severely reduced viability during development of hCSP-L115 and -L116 animals in comparison to WT hCSPα expression (p<0.0001; Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 3A.

claim: Adult L115- and L116-mutant escapers were initially sluggish in comparison to WT hCSPα but improved within ~10 days and exhibited a normal lifespan.
source: Adult L115- and L116-mutant escapers were initially sluggish in comparison to WT hCSPα but improved within ~10 days and exhibited a normal lifespan (not shown), which may be due to a decrease in the elav-driven expression.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: There was no significant difference in the viability between L115 and L116 mutant animals.
source: There was no significant difference in the viability between L115 and L116 mutant animals (p=0.91; Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα with the pan-neuronal nSyb-Gal4 driver caused a dose-dependent lethality similar to that of the elav-Gal4 driver.
source: Expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα with the pan-neuronal nSyb-Gal4 driver also caused a dose-dependent lethality, which was similar to that of the elav-Gal4 driver (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: CLN4 mutant adult escapers with nSyb-driven expression were very sluggish and hardly moved.
source: In contrast to the elav-driven expression, CLN4 mutant adult escapers were very sluggish and hardly moved.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: CLN4 mutant adult escapers with nSyb-driven expression were unable to properly inflate their wings.
source: They were also unable to properly inflate their wings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and died prematurely within 1–3 days.
evidence: Demonstrated by images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: High-level expression of WT hCSPα in the eye had essentially no effect at 23°C or 28°C in comparison to non-expressing control.
source: High-level expression of WT hCSPα from a line with multiple transgene insertions (see Materials and methods) had essentially no effect at 23°C or 28°C in comparison to non-expressing control (p>0.9; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by eye phenotype data in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Expression of hCSP-L116 at 23°C severely impaired the size, integrity, and pigmentation of the eye.
source: In comparison, expression of hCSP-L116 at 23°C severely impaired the size, integrity, and pigmentation of the eye (p<0.0001; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by eye phenotype data in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Raising flies at 28°C enhanced the severity of the degenerative phenotype of L116-mutant eyes.
source: Raising flies at 28°C to increase Gal4 activity and thereby gene expression enhanced the severity of the degenerative phenotype of L116-mutant eyes (p<0.0001; Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by eye phenotype data in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Levels of mutant hCSP-L115 and -L116 were significantly reduced at synaptic boutons in comparison to WT hCSPα.
source: In comparison to WT hCSPα, levels of mutant hCSP-L115 and -L116 were significantly reduced at synaptic boutons (p<0.013; Figure 4A,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 4A, H.

claim: Expression of CLN4 mutant or WT hCSPα had no effect on synaptic levels of endogenous WT dCSP at NMJs.
source: Expression of CLN4 mutant or WT hCSPα had no effect on synaptic levels of endogenous WT dCSP at NMJs (p>0.6; Figure 4A,I).

claim: hCSP-L115 and -L116 were enriched in brightly stained clusters that were more distant from the presynaptic membrane.

evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining images in Figure 4A, C.

claim: CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulated abnormally in axons of segmental nerves.
source: In comparison to control, CLN4 mutant hCSPα also accumulated abnormally in axons of segmental nerves (Figure 4G) and the larval brain (p<0.009; Figure 4B,J; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulated abnormally in the larval brain.
source: In comparison to control, CLN4 mutant hCSPα also accumulated abnormally in axons of segmental nerves (Figure 4G) and the larval brain (p<0.009; Figure 4B,J; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining images and quantification in Figure 4B, J.

claim: The size of CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulations in the larval brain ranged from ~500 nm in diameter to ~3 μm.
source: The size of CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulations in the larval brain was heterogeneous, ranging from ~500 nm in diameter to ~3 μm.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The occurrence of abnormal hCSP-L115 and -L116 accumulations was dose-dependent.
source: The occurrence of abnormal hCSP-L115 and -L116 accumulations was dose-dependent (not shown), which was most pronounced in axons of segmental nerves (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with reference to Figure 4G.

claim: CLN4 mutations reduce synaptic levels of hCSPα and cause a severe mislocalization.
source: Hence, CLN4 mutations reduce synaptic levels of hCSPα and cause a severe mislocalization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immunostaining data.

claim: A fraction of the abnormal accumulations of hCSP-L115 and -L116 in axons and somata contained significant amounts of endogenous WT dCSP.
source: A fraction of the abnormal accumulations of hCSP-L115 and -L116 in axons (not shown) and somata (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) contained significant amounts of endogenous WT dCSP.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 4E.

claim: Essentially all CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulations were immunopositive for ubiquitinated proteins in somata and synaptic boutons of NMJs.
source: Indeed, essentially all CLN4 mutant hCSPα accumulations were immunopositive for ubiquitinated proteins in somata and synaptic boutons of NMJs (Figure 4D,F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 4D, F.

claim: The amount of hCSPα accumulations containing ubiquitinated proteins was significantly increased in CLN4 mutants in comparison to larvae expressing WT hCSPα.
source: In comparison to larvae expressing WT hCSPα, the amount of hCSPα accumulations containing ubiquitinated proteins was significantly increased in CLN4 mutants (p<0.001; Figure 4K).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in Figure 4K.

claim: The amount of ubiquitinated protein foci that were not associated with mutant hCSPα was significantly increased in brains expressing hCSPα-L115 or -L116.
source: In comparison, the amount of ubiquitinated protein foci that were not associated with mutant hCSPα was significantly increased in brains expressing hCSPα-L115 or -L116 (p<0.03; Figure 4L).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in Figure 4L.

claim: CLN4 mutant hCSPα may directly or indirectly affect a step of protein homeostasis that leads to excessive protein ubiquitination of unrelated proteins.
source: Hence, CLN4 mutant hCSPα may directly or indirectly affect a step of protein homeostasis that that leads to excessive protein ubiquitination of unrelated proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of increased ubiquitinated proteins not associated with mutant hCSPα.

claim: Neuronal KD of TSG101 caused a mislocalization of endogenous dCSP, which accumulated on HRS-positive endosomes in the neuropil and neuronal somata of the larval VNC.
source: Neuronal KD of TSG101 caused a mislocalization of endogenous dCSP, which accumulated on HRS-positive endosomes in the neuropil and neuronal somata of the larval VNC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Abnormal dCSP accumulations were present in central regions of synaptic boutons of larval NMJs after TSG101 KD.
source: Abnormal dCSP accumulations were also present in central regions of synaptic boutons of larval NMJs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WT CSP is likely being degraded through the endo-lysosomal pathway.
source: Hence, WT CSP is likely being degraded though the endo-lysosomal pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of dCSP on HRS-positive endosomes after TSG101 KD.

claim: KD of TSG101 did not cause the formation of high-molecular weight dCSP oligomers.
source: In contrast to hCSPα-L115 and -L116 expression, KD of TSG101 did not cause the formation of high-molecular weight dCSP oligomers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that CSP oligomer formation is independent of impaired ESCRT function.
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CSP oligomer formation is independent of impaired ESCRT function.
source: In contrast to hCSPα-L115 and -L116 expression, KD of TSG101 did not cause the formation of high-molecular weight dCSP oligomers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that CSP oligomer formation is independent of impaired ESCRT function.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of oligomerization after TSG101 KD.

claim: Impaired prelysosomal ESCRT function had no effect on the palmitoylation state of dCSP.
source: In contrast to a recent report showing that impaired lysosomal activity in mouse neurons decreases CSPα's palmitoylation (Sambri et al., 2017), impaired prelysosomal ESCRT function had no effect on the palmitoylation state of dCSP.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation that contrasts with a cited study.

claim: Reducing endogenous WT dCSP levels by expressing two transgenic copies of CLN4 mutant hCSP in heterozygous dcsp deletion mutants significantly suppressed the lethality induced by CLN4 mutations.
source: Reducing endogenous WT dCSP levels by expressing two transgenic copies of CLN4 mutant hCSP in heterozygous dcsp deletion mutants significantly suppressed the lethality induced by CLN4 mutations such that significantly more animals reached adulthood (p<0.02, Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 7A.

claim: Increasing levels of WT hCSPα by co-expressing WT hCSPα with either one copy of hCSP-L115 or -L116 significantly reduced viability to ~54% and 48%, respectively.
source: Conversely, increasing levels of WT hCSPα by co-expressing WT hCSPα with either one copy of hCSP-L115 or -L116 significantly reduced viability to ~54% and 48%, respectively (p<0.001, Figure 7B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 7B-C.

claim: The lethality induced by co-expression of WT and CLN4 mutant hCSPα was significantly higher than the lethality induced by two copy expression of WT hCSPα.
source: The lethality induced by co-expression of WT and CLN4 mutant hCSPα was significantly higher than the lethality induced by two copy expression of WT hCSPα (p<0.03, Figure 7B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 7B-C.

claim: The modulating effects of altered WT dCSP or hCSPα levels on L115- and L116-induced lethality essentially exclude the possibility that either mutation acts as a dominant-negative.
source: Hence, the modulating effects of altered WT dCSP or hCSPα levels on L115- and L116-induced lethality essentially exclude the possibility that either mutation acts as a dominant-negative.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on genetic interaction data.

claim: The modulating effects of altered WT CSP levels are consistent with the genetic characteristics of a hypermorphic GOF mutation.
source: Instead, these effects are consistent with the genetic characteristics of a hypermorphic GOF mutation (Muller, 1932; Wilkie, 1994).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on genetic interaction data and cited genetic principles.

claim: Reducing WT dCSP levels by expressing CLN4 mutant hCSPα in hetero- or homozygous dcsp deletion mutants significantly attenuated the levels of SDS-resistant hCSP-L116 and -L115 oligomers.
source: Reducing WT dCSP levels by expressing CLN4 mutant hCSPα in hetero- or homozygous dcsp deletion mutants significantly attenuated the levels of SDS-resistant hCSP-L116 and -L115 oligomers (p<0.05; Figure 7D,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7D, F.

claim: Increasing WT dCSP levels by co-expressing a WT transgene together with a single CLN4 mutant transgene increased the amount of hCSP-L115 and L116 oligomers.
source: Conversely, increasing WT dCSP levels by co-expressing a WT transgene together with a single CLN4 mutant transgene increased the amount of hCSP-L115 and L116 oligomers (p<0.007, Figure 7D,I).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7D, I.

claim: Coexpression of WT hCSPα significantly increased oligomerization of both hCSP-L116 and -L115.
source: Coexpression of WT hCSPα also significantly increased oligomerization of both hCSP-L116 and -L115 (p<0.008; Figure 7E,L).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7E, L.

claim: High-level overexpression of WT hCSPα from two transgenes did not induce significant oligomerization.
source: In comparison, high-level overexpression of WT hCSPα from two transgenes did not induce significant oligomerization (Figures 7E and 2A,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot data in Figures 7E and 2A, C.

claim: Reducing or even abolishing WT dCSP levels had no effect on the levels of lipidated monomeric hCSP-L115 and -L116.
source: In contrast to the modulatory effects of WT CSP on mutant hCSPα oligomer levels, reducing or even abolishing WT dCSP levels had no effect on the levels of lipidated monomeric hCSP-L115 and -L116 (p>0.4; Figure 7G).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7G.

claim: Coexpressing WT dCSP2 or hCSPα with CLN4 mutant hCSPα increased lipidated mutant hCSPα monomers.
source: Coexpressing WT dCSP2 or hCSPα with CLN4 mutant hCSPα increased lipidated mutant hCSPα monomers (p<0.05; Figure 7J,M).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7J, M.

claim: WT hCSPα may stabilize CLN4 mutant hCSPα monomers.
source: Notably, coexpression of WT hCSPα increased lipidated hCSP-L115 and -L116 monomers to levels that were similar to those of two copy WT hCSPα expression (Figure 7M). This indicates that WT hCSPα may stabilize CLN4 mutant hCSPα monomers.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in lipidated mutant monomers upon WT hCSPα coexpression.

claim: Reducing dCSP levels by one gene copy significantly suppressed the endosomal accumulation of both hCSP-L115 and -L116 in larval VNCs.
source: Indeed, reducing dCSP levels by one gene copy significantly suppressed the endosomal accumulation of both hCSP-L115 and -L116 in larval VNCs (p<0.05; Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Reducing dCSP gene dosage decreased the amount of accumulating ubiquitinated proteins in the larval VNC.
source: Reducing dCSP gene dosage also decreased the amount of accumulating ubiquitinated proteins in the larval VNC (p<0.04; Figure 8C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 8C.

claim: Reduced dCSP levels significantly enhanced the already reduced synaptic protein levels of hCSP-L115 and -L116 at larval NMJs.
source: However, reduced dCSP levels significantly enhanced the already reduced synaptic protein levels of hCSP-L115 and -L116 at larval NMJs (p<0.03; Figure 8D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 8D.

claim: The modulating effects of altering WT fly and human CSP levels on L115- and L116-induced phenotypes suggest that the hCSP-L115 and -L116 alleles are hypermorphic gain of function mutations that increase an intrinsic activity.
source: Taken together, the modulating effects of altering WT fly and human CSP levels on L115- and L116-induced phenotypes in viability, mutant hCSPα oligomerization, accumulation on endosomes and ubiquitinated proteins suggest that the hCSP-L115 and -L116 alleles are hypermorphic gain of function mutations that increase an intrinsic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple genetic interaction experiments.

claim: These findings uncover a correlation between the reduced viability of CLN4 mutant flies, the degree of mutant hCSPα oligomerization and the failure of degrading oligomers.
source: In addition, these findings uncover a correlation between the reduced viability of CLN4 mutant flies, the degree of mutant hCSPα oligomerization and the failure of degrading oligomers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: Reducing the gene dosage of hsc4 by expressing mutant hCSP-L115 or L116 in heterozygous hsc4∆356 deletion mutants significantly suppressed their lethality.
source: Reducing the gene dosage of hsc4 by expressing mutant hCSP-L115 or L116 in heterozygous hsc4∆356 deletion mutants significantly suppressed their lethality (p<0.0001; Figure 9F).
evidence: Demonstrated by viability data in Figure 9F.

claim: Hsc4 contributes to the toxicity of CLN4 mutations.
source: Hence, Hsc4 contributes to the toxicity of CLN4 mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the suppression of lethality by reduced Hsc4 levels.

claim: Hsc4 OE had no significant effects on the amount of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers, monomers and overall protein levels.
source: Hsc4 OE had no significant effects on the amount of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers, monomers and overall protein levels (p>0.05; Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Reducing Hsc4 levels by expressing mutant hCSP-L115 or L116 in heterozygous hsc4∆356 deletion mutants significantly reduced the amount of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers.
source: However, reducing Hsc4 levels by expressing mutant hCSP-L115 or L116 in heterozygous hsc4∆356 deletion mutants significantly reduced the amount of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers (p<0.02; Figure 9B–C,G) but had no differential effects (p>0.8).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 9B-C, G.

claim: Reducing Hsc4 levels reduced the levels of lipidated and non-lipidated hCSP-L115 and -L116 monomers, as well as overall protein levels.
source: It also reduced the levels of lipidated and non-lipidated hCSP-L115 and -L116 monomers, as well as overall protein levels (p<0.05; Figure 9H–J).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 9H-J.

claim: Reducing Hsc4 levels had no effect on the levels of monomeric WT hCSPα.
source: However, this is unlikely the case since reducing Hsc4 levels had no effect on the levels of monomeric WT hCSPα (Figure 9K), which was consistent with the normal dCSP levels observed in hsc4 deletion mutants (Bronk et al., 2001).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 9K.

claim: Reducing Hsc4 levels suppressed the amount of hCSP-L115 and -L116 protein accumulations on endosomes in the larval VNC.
source: Reducing Hsc4 levels also suppressed the amount of hCSP-L115 and -L116 protein accumulations on endosomes in the larval VNC (p<0.05; Figure 9L and Figure 9—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 9L.

claim: Reducing Hsc4 levels suppressed the amount of ubiquitinated protein accumulations induced by hCSP-L116.
source: It also suppressed the amount of ubiquitinated protein accumulations induced by hCSP-L116 (p<0.05) but had no effect on L115-induced levels (p=0.8; Figure 9M).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 9M.

claim: Reducing hsc4 gene dosage had no effect on the synaptic levels of hCSP-L116 at larval NMJs.
source: Reducing hsc4 gene dosage had no effect on the synaptic levels of hCSP-L116 at larval NMJs (p=0.7; Figure 9N).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 9N.

claim: Reducing hsc4 gene dosage further lowered the synaptic levels of hCSP-L115.
source: However, it further lowered the synaptic levels of hCSP-L115 (p<0.01; Figure 9N).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining quantification in Figure 9N.

claim: HA-tagged Hsc4 colocalized with the abnormal accumulations of hCSP-L115 and -L116.
source: Since HA-tagged Hsc4 colocalized with the abnormal accumulations of hCSP-L115 and -L116 (Figure 9O), it may interfere with the prelysosomal trafficking and subsequent degradation of mutant hCSPα.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 9O.

claim: Hsc4 may interfere with the prelysosomal trafficking and subsequent degradation of mutant hCSPα.
source: Since HA-tagged Hsc4 colocalized with the abnormal accumulations of hCSP-L115 and -L116 (Figure 9O), it may interfere with the prelysosomal trafficking and subsequent degradation of mutant hCSPα.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the colocalization data.

claim: Lower Hsc4 levels reduced the overall protein levels of mutant but not WT hCSPα.
source: Consistently, lower Hsc4 levels reduced the overall protein levels of mutant but not WT hCSPα (Figure 9J–K).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 9J-K.

claim: The suppression effects of a reduced hsc4 gene dosage on the oligomerization and abnormal accumulation of CLN4 mutant hCSPα on endosomes suggest that Hsc4 significantly contributes to this pathology.
source: In conclusion, the suppression effects of a reduced hsc4 gene dosage on the oligomerization and abnormal accumulation of CLN4 mutant hCSPα on endosomes suggest that Hsc4 significantly contributes to this pathology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction data with Hsc4.

claim: Neuronal expression of either mutant hCSPα or dCSP mirrored all key pathological features of post-mortem human CLN4 brains.
source: Neuronal expression of either mutant hCSPα or dCSP mirrored key pathological features of post-mortem human CLN4 brains, including reduced levels of palmitoylated hCSPα monomers and excessive formation of oligomers.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the biochemical data.

claim: Only ubiquitinated mutant hCSPα oligomers were detected but no ubiquitinated monomers.
source: Consistent with the idea that ubiquitination is likely a consequence of oligomerization, only ubiquitinated mutant hCSPα oligomers were detected but no ubiquitinated monomers.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The L115 mutation had stronger effects than L116.
source: In general, the L115 mutation had stronger effects than L116, which has also been observed in post mortem brains and mammalian cell cultures (Diez-Ardanuy et al., 2017; Greaves et al., 2012; Henderson et al., 2016; Zhang and Chandra, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary observation supported by data and citations.

claim: Expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα or dCSP in fly neurons provides a valid CLN4 disease model.
source: Accordingly, expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα or dCSP in fly neurons provides a valid CLN4 disease model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the recapitulation of key pathological features.

claim: Single copy expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα did not cause detectable degeneration or lethality, even though significant levels of ubiquitinated hCSPα oligomers and abnormal prelysosomal accumulations of hCSPα were present.
source: Single copy expression of CLN4 mutant hCSPα did not cause detectable degeneration or lethality, even though significant levels of ubiquitinated hCSPα oligomers and abnormal prelysosomal accumulations of hCSPα were present.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental observations.

claim: The significant drop in viability indicated a sharp threshold of neurotoxicity, which was correlated with an increase in the levels of hCSPα oligomers and prelysosomal accumulations.
source: The significant drop in viability indicated a sharp threshold of neurotoxicity, which was correlated with an increase in the levels of hCSPα oligomers and prelysosomal accumulations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dose-dependent viability data.

claim: The build-up of pathological features in the CLN4 fly model agrees with the assumed general concept of late onset neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The build-up of these pathological features in the CLN4 fly model agrees with the assumed general concept of late onset neurodegenerative diseases, which typically show a progressive accumulation of protein aggregates and defects in protein homeostasis over a long period that is met by a declining age-dependent capacity of protein homeostasis (Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to general concepts in the field supported by a citation.

claim: CLN4 mutations may primarily impair palmitoylation of the CS domain.
source: In principle, there are two possibilities how CLN4 mutations may mislocalize CSP: 1) CLN4 mutations may primarily impair palmitoylation of the CS domain, which is required for ER and Golgi exit, and for a stable association with SVPs and/or SVs (Greaves and Chamberlain, 2006; Greaves et al., 2008; Ohyama et al., 2007; Stowers and Isacoff, 2007).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis but then argued against.

claim: CLN4 mutations primarily impairing palmitoylation is unlikely because mutant hCSPα was not detectable in the ER or Golgi of fly neurons.
source: However, this possibility is unlikely the case since mutant hCSPα was not detectable in the ER or Golgi of fly neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on immunostaining data.

claim: CLN4 mutations may primarily induce oligomerization by exaggerating the dimerization properties of the CS domain.
source: 2) CLN4 mutations may primarily induce oligomerization by exaggerating the dimerization properties of the CS domain (Xu et al., 2010) such that self-association leads mostly to misfolded high-molecular weight oligomers.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Oligomerization of CLN4 mutant hCSPα can be suppressed by alanine or leucine substitutions of a cluster of palmitoylated cysteines (C122-125) located next to the L115/116 mutations.
source: Notably, oligomerization of CLN4 mutant hCSPα can be suppressed by alanine or leucine substitutions of a cluster of palmitoylated cysteines (C122-125) located next to the L115/116 mutations (Diez-Ardanuy et al., 2017), which is consistent with the idea that CLN4 mutations primarily induce oligomerization.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: The oligomerization of mutant hCSPα is apparently triggered after exiting the Golgi, either during its association with SVPs, or after arriving at axon terminals and associating with SVs.
source: In fly neurons, the oligomerization of mutant hCSPα is apparently triggered after exiting the Golgi, either during its association with SVPs, or after arriving at axon terminals and associating with SVs.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data.

claim: Mutant hCSPα oligomers are potentially re-routed from both SVPs and SVs because some mutant hCSPα colocalizes with SVs at axon terminals.
source: Mutant hCSPα oligomers are potentially re-routed from both SVPs and SVs because some mutant hCSPα colocalizes with SVs at axon terminals.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data.

claim: The ubiquitination of CLN4 mutant hCSPα oligomers likely indicates that they are misfolded and thus targets for ubiquitination and degradation like other misfolded proteins.
source: The ubiquitination of CLN4 mutant hCSPα oligomers likely indicates that they are misfolded and thus targets for ubiquitination and degradation like other misfolded proteins (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on general knowledge about protein quality control.

claim: Ubiquitinated mutant hCSPα oligomers are sorted into the endolysosomal pathway if they remain associated with membranes.
source: Since WT dCSP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and hCSPα are mostly degraded by lysosomes (Benitez and Sands, 2017; Chapel et al., 2013; Sambri et al., 2017; Schröder et al., 2007; Tharkeshwar et al., 2017), one expects that ubiquitinated mutant hCSPα oligomers are sorted into the endolysosomal pathway if they remain associated with membranes. This appears to be the case since the majority of abnormal mutant hCSPα accumulations in fly neurons represented prelysosomal endosomes, which were defined by the colocalization of ubiquitinated proteins and the prelysosomal markers LAMP1-GFP and HRS.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data and cited knowledge about CSP degradation.

claim: CLN4 mutations may primarily induce oligomerization of membrane-associated hCSPα, which causes ubiquitination and re-routing into lysosomal pathways.
source: Hence, these data suggest that CLN4 mutations may primarily induce oligomerization of membrane-associated hCSPα, which causes ubiquitination and re-routing into lysosomal pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Axonal prelysosomal endosomes containing mutant hCSPα are likely retrogradely trafficked for lysosomal processing since degradative lysosomes containing cathepsin B/D are essentially absent from distal axons.
source: Axonal prelysosomal endosomes containing mutant hCSPα are likely retrogradely trafficked for lysosomal processing since degradative lysosomes containing cathepsin B/D are essentially absent from distal axons (Cai et al., 2010; Cheng et al., 2018; Gowrishankar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from cited knowledge about lysosome distribution in axons.

claim: Both the axonal trafficking as well as the maturation of prelysosomal endosomes containing mutant hCSPα are potentially impaired.
source: Both the axonal trafficking as well as the maturation of prelysosomal endosomes containing mutant hCSPα are potentially impaired.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed accumulations.

claim: A physical defect in axonal trafficking is indicated by the large size of the hCSPα accumulations and by the frequent occurrence of large and abnormal EM-dense membrane structures in axons of CLN4 mutants.
source: A physical defect in axonal trafficking is indicated by the large size of the hCSPα accumulations and by the frequent occurrence of large and abnormal EM-dense membrane structures in axons of CLN4 mutants, which have the potential to 'clog' axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the microscopy data.

claim: A reduced efficiency in the maturation of mutant hCSPα-positive prelysosomal endosomes is indicated by their abnormally large size and by their failure to co-label with the PI3P lipid reporter FYVE-GFP.
source: A reduced efficiency in the maturation of mutant hCSPα-positive prelysosomal endosomes is indicated by their abnormally large size and by their failure to co-label with the PI3P lipid reporter FYVE-GFP.
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data.

claim: It is possible that mutant hCSPα may impair the transition from early to late endosomes.
source: Since only a small number of mutant hCSPα accumulations co-localized with the early endosome marker Rab5 but essentially no accumulations colocalized with the late endosomal or lysosomal markers Rab7 and spinster, it is possible that mutant hCSPα may impair the transition from early to late endosomes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the colocalization data.

claim: The frequent occurrence of abnormal, multi-laminar structures containing EM-dense membranes and abnormal autophagosome-like structures indicate that CLN4 mutations impair steps of membrane trafficking in axons and somata.
source: The frequent occurrence of abnormal, multi-laminar structures containing EM-dense membranes and abnormal autophagosome-like structures further indicate that CLN4 mutations impair steps of membrane trafficking in axons and somata.
evidence: This is inferred from the electron microscopy data.

claim: The abnormal endosomal membranes of CLN4 mutants suggest a defect in prelysosomal trafficking.
source: Since similar ultrastructural defects were observed after disruption of ESCRT function (Doyotte et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007), the abnormal endosomal membranes of CLN4 mutants suggest a defect in prelysosomal trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred by comparison to cited studies on ESCRT mutants.

claim: At least some of the abnormal membrane structures of CLN4 mutants could be the consequence of defects in the unconventional secretion of misfolded cytosolic proteins.
source: Alternatively, at least some of the abnormal membrane structures of CLN4 mutants could be the consequence of defects in the unconventional secretion of misfolded cytosolic proteins, which is facilitated by CSP proteins at least in non-neuronal cells (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited knowledge about CSP function.

claim: The excessive ubiquitination may be a secondary consequence of the prelysosomal trafficking defects induced by CLN4 mutations.
source: Hence, the excessive ubiquitination may be a secondary consequence of the prelysosomal trafficking defects induced by CLN4 mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data.

claim: The pathological mechanisms underlying CLN4 appear to be different from those of most other NCLs.
source: The pathological mechanisms underlying CLN4 appear to be different from those of most other NCLs, which are typically due to loss of function mutations in genes that mediate lysosomal function, ER-lysosomal trafficking, or protein lipidation (Cárcel-Trullols et al., 2015; Cooper et al., 2015; Cotman et al., 2013; Mole and Cotman, 2015; Warrier et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to other NCLs based on cited knowledge.

claim: The pathological mechanisms underlying CLN4 appear similar to those of 'classical' neurodegenerative diseases that are induced by a progressive build-up of protein oligomers/aggregates.
source: As such, the pathological mechanisms underlying CLN4 appear similar to those of 'classical' neurodegenerative diseases that are induced by a progressive build-up of protein oligomers/aggregates that then leads to a failure of protein homeostasis and/or lysosomal pathways (Abramov et al., 2009; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015; Lansbury and Lashuel, 2006; Muchowski and Wacker, 2005; Neefjes and van der Kant, 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to other neurodegenerative diseases based on cited knowledge.

claim: The fly model provides a valuable tool for future work to dissect pathological mechanisms underlying CLN4.
source: While we are just beginning to understand the complicated nature of CLN4, the fly model provides a valuable tool for future work to dissect pathological mechanisms underlying CLN4.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the utility of the model.

claim: Levels of lipidated monomeric WT hCSPα were estimated to be 0.98 ± 0.23 times of endogenous dCSP levels when expressed from a single transgene with an elav-Gal4 driver.
source: When expressed from a single transgene with an elav-Gal4 driver, lipidated monomeric protein levels of WT hCSPα were estimated to be 0.98 ± 0.23 times of endogenous dCSP levels (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental measurement.

claim: Mutant hCSPα was not detectable in the ER or Golgi of fly neurons.
source: However, this possibility is unlikely the case since mutant hCSPα was not detectable in the ER or Golgi of fly neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from immunostaining.

claim: Mutant hCSPα accumulations did not colocalize with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), cis-, or trans-Golgi complexes.
source: Mutant hCSPα accumulations did not colocalize with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), cis-, or trans-Golgi complexes (Figure 5A), which excluded a major defect in ER or Golgi trafficking.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 5A.

claim: A large fraction of mutant hCSPα co-accumulated with hLAMP1-GFP.
source: A large fraction of mutant hCSPα co-accumulated with hLAMP1-GFP (Figure 5B–C), which labels a heterogeneous population of organelles ranging from pre-degradative endosomal species to degradative lysosome (Cheng et al., 2018; Saftig and Klumperman, 2009; Yap et al., 2018).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining quantification in Figure 5B-C.

claim: A similar large fraction of mutant hCSPα co-accumulated with HRS.
source: A similar large fraction of mutant hCSPα co-accumulated with hepatocyte growth factor regulated tyrosine kinase substrate (HRS, Figure 5C,E), which is a critical component of 'endosomal sorting complexes required for transport' (ESCRT) mediating the transition from early to late endosomes (Raiborg and Stenmark, 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining quantification in Figure 5C, E.

claim: Only a small fraction of mutant hCSPα co-localized with coexpressed Rab5-GFP or the autophagosomal marker ATG8/LC3-GFP.
source: Only a small fraction co-localized with coexpressed Rab5-GFP (not shown) or the autophagosomal marker ATG8/LC3-GFP (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 5D.

claim: No co-localization of mutant hCSPα was observed with lysosomal Spinster-GFP or the late endosomal protein Rab7.
source: No co-localization was observed with lysosomal Spinster-GFP (Figure 5B; Rong et al., 2011; Sweeney and Davis, 2002) or the late endosomal protein Rab7 (not shown; Guerra and Bucci, 2016).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 5B.

claim: Endosomes accumulating mutant hCSPα did not co-localize with the co-expressed phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) sensor FYVE-GFP.
source: Notably, endosomes accumulating mutant hCSPα did not co-localize with the co-expressed phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) sensor FYVE-GFP (Figure 5B), even though HRS requires PI3P for membrane association (Mayers et al., 2013; Raiborg et al., 2001a).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 5B.

claim: HRS colocalized with mutant hCSPα at synaptic boutons of NMJs.
source: Consistent with the colocalization of mutant hCSPα with ubiquitinated proteins at axon terminals (Figure 4F), HRS also colocalized with mutant hCSPα at synaptic boutons of NMJs (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining in Figure 5F.

claim: hCSPα-positive accumulations co-localized with SV-associated Synaptobrevin-GFP.
source: Consistently, hCSPα-positive accumulations co-localized with SV-associated Synaptobrevin-GFP (Syb-GFP; Figure 5C,G) while a small subset co-localized with the synaptic plasma membrane protein Syntaxin 1A (not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunostaining quantification in Figure 5C, G.

claim: The CSPα chaperone clients Dynamin and SNAP-25 did not co-localize with hCSPα-positive endosomes.
source: The CSPα chaperone clients Dynamin and SNAP-25 (Sharma et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012) did not co-localize with hCSPα-positive endosomes (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The most prominent and frequent abnormal structures in CLN4 mutants were multilamellar 'membrane whirls' of various shapes and density that contain highly electron-dense membranes.
source: The most prominent and frequent abnormal structures were multilamellar 'membrane whirls' of various shapes and density that contain highly electron-dense membranes (arrowheads, Figure 6A–B,C–D,F–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 6.

claim: Membrane whirls were most frequently observed in the neuropil of the VNC and axons of segmental nerves.
source: Like endosomal hCSPα-positive accumulations detected by confocal microscopy, membrane whirls were most frequently observed in the neuropil of the VNC and axons of segmental nerves (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 6C-D.

claim: A number of secondary (residual) lysosomes and abnormal autophagosome- and/or amphisome-like structures were present in CLN4 mutants.
source: In addition to electron-dense membrane whirls, a number of secondary (residual) lysosomes (Figure 6A,E) and abnormal autophagosome- and/or amphisome-like structures were present (white arrowhead, Figure 6F–I).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 6.

claim: EM-dense membranes forming whirls may interact with autophagosomes.
source: Interestingly, EM-dense membranes forming whirls may interact with autophagosomes (arrow, Figure 6G).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy image in Figure 6G.

claim: Homogenous electron-dense accumulations of unknown nature were frequently present in cellular regions of CLN4 mutant larval brains.
source: Next to abnormal membranes structures, homogenous electron-dense accumulations of unknown nature were frequently present in cellular regions of CLN4 mutant larval brains (arrow, Figure 6B,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 6B, H.

claim: A number of neurons that contained abnormal membrane structures also exhibited a severe fragmentation of the nuclear envelope and bloated Golgi cisternae.
source: Finally, a number of neurons that contained abnormal membrane structures also exhibited a severe fragmentation of the nuclear envelope and bloated Golgi cisternae (Figure 6B), which together likely indicate a late stage of neuronal dysfunction and neurodegeneration (Nixon, 2006).
evidence: Demonstrated by electron microscopy image in Figure 6B.

claim: Reducing the gene dosage of hsc4 by expressing mutant hCSP-L116 in heterozygous hsc4∆356 deletion mutants significantly suppressed both the structural and depigmentation defects of L116 mutant eyes.
source: Reducing endogenous Hsc70-4 (Hsc4) levels by expressing hCSP-L116 in heterozygous hsc4∆356 deletion mutants (Bronk et al., 2001) significantly suppressed both the structural and depigmentation defects of L116 mutant eyes (p=0.005; Figure 9A,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by eye phenotype data in Figure 9A, E.

claim: Co-expression of a UAS hairpin transgene knocking down Hsc4 suppressed the L116 eye phenotype.
source: Co-expression of a UAS hairpin transgene knocking down Hsc4 also suppressed the L116 eye phenotype (p=0.007; Figure 9A,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by eye phenotype data in Figure 9A, E.

claim: Reducing the gene dosage of Hsc70-3 or Hsc70-5 had no effect on L116 eye phenotypes.
source: However, reducing the gene dosage of Hsc70-3 or Hsc70-5 had no effect (not shown), indicating that the suppression of L116-mutant eye phenotypes by reduced levels of Hsc4 is not a general effect of Hsc70 proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Co-expression of either Syntaxin 1A (Syx1A) or neuronal Synaptobrevin (nSyb) with hCSP-L116 enhanced the L116 eye phenotype.
source: Co-expression of either Syntaxin 1A (Syx1A) or neuronal Synaptobrevin (nSyb) with hCSP-L116 enhanced the L116 eye phenotype (p<0.01; Figure 9A,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by eye phenotype data in Figure 9A, D.

claim: Overexpression or RNAi-mediated knockdown of SNAP25 had no effect on L116 eye phenotypes.
source: Overexpression or RNAi-mediated knockdown of SNAP25 had no effect (not shown), even though a heterozygous deletion of SNAP25 enhanced degenerative phenotypes of hCSPα knockout mice (Sharma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Individual overexpression of Syntaxin 1A (Syx1A), neuronal Synaptobrevin (nSyb), or SNAP25 had no effect on the eye.
source: Individual overexpression of Syntaxin 1A (Syx1A), neuronal Synaptobrevin (nSyb), or SNAP25 had no effect on the eye (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Elav-driven neuronal expression of WT hCSPα from a single transgene had no effect on adult lifespan.
source: Elav-driven neuronal expression of WT or CLN4 mutant hCSPα from a single transgene had no effect on viability during development (Figure 3A) and adult lifespan (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: CLN4 mutant adult escapers with nSyb-driven expression died prematurely within 1–3 days.
source: They were also unable to properly inflate their wings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and died prematurely within 1–3 days.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Levels of non-lipidated CLN4 mutant hCSP were unaffected by reducing the gene dosage of endogenous WT dCSP2.
source: Levels of non-lipidated monomeric CLN4 mutant hCSP were unaffected by reducing the gene dosage of endogenous WT dCSP2 (p>0.3; Figure 7H).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7H.

claim: Coexpression of either WT dCSP2 or hCSPα with CLN4 mutant hCSPα increased levels of non-lipidated mutant hCSPα monomers.
source: However, coexpression of either WT dCSP2 or hCSPα with CLN4 mutant hCSPα increased levels of non-lipidated mutant hCSPα monomers (p<0.05; Figure 7K,N).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7K, N.

claim: The increase in non-lipidated mutant monomers induced by WT hCSPα was non-additive since it was significantly larger than the increase induced by doubling WT hCSPα expression.
source: At least the increase induced by WT hCSPα was non-additive since it was significantly larger than the increase induced by doubling WT hCSPα expression (p<0.013; Figure 7N).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7N.

claim: Increased levels of WT CSP may outcompete CLN4 mutant hCSPα for palmitoylation or promote its depalmitoylation.
source: Hence, increased levels of WT CSP may outcompete CLN4 mutant hCSPα for palmitoylation or, alternatively, promote its depalmitoylation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the non-additive increase in non-lipidated monomers.

claim: Levels of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers were attenuated to a similar degree by reducing WT dCSP levels.
source: Levels of hCSP-L116 and -L115 oligomers were attenuated to a similar degree (p>0.5; Figure 7F).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 7F.

claim: Reducing Hsc4 levels had no differential effects on hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomer reduction.
source: However, reducing Hsc4 levels by expressing mutant hCSP-L115 or L116 in heterozygous hsc4∆356 deletion mutants significantly reduced the amount of hCSP-L115 and -L116 oligomers (p<0.02; Figure 9B–C,G) but had no differential effects (p>0.8).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot quantification in Figure 9B-C, G.
